description: FIRST LOFT GOLDEN (the second NON-PRISMATIC feature): a 20x20 mm square section on the XY datum plane lofted (ruled) down to a single APEX point 30 mm up the +Z axis -> a right square pyramid. A THREE-feature TREE (base sketch -> apex sketch -> loft) evaluated through the same evaluate-tree path as the sweep/extrude goldens: planegcs solves BOTH sketches -> the base square wire assembles + closes (SHARED build_profile_face -> outer_wire) while the apex sketch's lone point becomes a single Vertex (build_loft_section, the apex branch) -> Solid.make_loft(ruled=True) skins the square-to-apex sections -> add against the (empty) body -> GProp -> tessellation -> content-addressed GLB. Locks: the loft handler + per-section FeatureRef resolution (the ordered profiles slot) + loft-to-apex (a point section) + ruled ThruSections skin + add boolean, GProp over 4 planar triangular sides + 1 square cap, planar-face tessellation, and (via the parametrized round-trip gate) STEP re-import of the lofted B-rep. WHY A PYRAMID, not the brief's cylinder/frustum: those need two PARALLEL offset circular sections, which v1 cannot author -- datum planes are origin-only and mutually PERPENDICULAR (never parallel), so two parallel offset sections do not exist until offset datum planes land. A square section lofted to an apex point IS authorable and is a PLANAR-faced solid with an exact analytic volume (a^2*h/3), so every mass property, topology count, and mesh count is HAND-DERIVABLE -- the strongest available loft golden. Cross-checked independently: this same solid built by build123d's Solid.make_cone-equivalent primitive path and by the analytic pyramid formulae agree to machine precision.
derivation: Expectations are HAND-DERIVED analytic values, not recorded harness output (geometry-gates skill: a golden recorded from buggy output enshrines the bug). Section 1 is an axis-aligned square, corners (+/-10, +/-10) mm on the XY datum plane (normal +Z, at world z=0), side a = 20 mm. Section 2 is a single sketch POINT at (0, 30) on the XZ datum plane; on XZ, sketch (x,y) maps to world (x,0,y), so it is the APEX vertex at world (0,0,30). Ruled-lofting the square to the apex yields a right square pyramid, base at z=0, apex on +Z at height H = 30 mm.

Both sketches return input positions bitwise. The base square is under-constrained (4 coincident corners + horizontal/vertical on the 4 edges pin its SHAPE and orientation but leave the whole-sketch position DOF free), so planegcs provably returns the drawn positions unchanged (status converged; same solver posture as the revolve/extrude goldens -- verified 2026-07-12, solved == input). The apex point is fully fixed (a `fixed` constraint at (0,30), 0 DOF). No solver error is introduced.
volume = (1/3) * base_area * H = (1/3) * a^2 * H = (1/3) * 400 * 30 = 4000 mm^3 exactly (the pyramid volume formula).

surface_area = base + 4 lateral triangles. base = a^2 = 400 mm^2. Each triangular side has base a = 20 and slant height = the apex-to-base-edge-midpoint distance: the y=-10 base edge has midpoint (0,-10,0); apex (0,0,30); slant = sqrt(0^2 + 10^2 + 30^2) = sqrt(1000) mm. One side = (1/2)*a*slant = (1/2)*20*sqrt(1000) = 10*sqrt(1000); four sides = 40*sqrt(1000) = 1264.9110640673518 mm^2. Total = 400 + 40*sqrt(1000) = 1664.9110640673516 mm^2 (nearest double).

centroid = (0, 0, H/4) = (0, 0, 7.5) mm: a solid pyramid's centroid sits at one quarter of the height above the base, on the axis of symmetry (the +Z axis through the base centre and the apex). (GProp puts x,y at ulp scale ~3e-16, z exactly 7.5.)
bounding_box = [-10,-10,0]..[10,10,30]: the base square spans +/-a/2 = +/-10 in x and y at z=0, and the sweep runs the full H up +Z to the apex at (0,0,30).

topology: a square pyramid is 5 faces (1 square base cap + 4 triangular sides), 8 edges (4 base edges + 4 lateral edges from each base corner to the apex), 1 closed shell. All faces are PLANAR (the ruled skin between a polygon and a point is flat-facetted), unlike the sweep/revolve goldens' curved cylinders -- so there is no seam edge and no periodic surface here.

mesh (linear 0.1 mm / angular 0.1 rad): every face is planar, so tessellation is trivial and deflection-independent. The square base triangulates to exactly 2 triangles over its 4 corners; each triangular side is 1 triangle over its 3 corners. Faceted per-face normals mean no vertex sharing across faces (same convention as the box golden): base 4 verts / 2 triangles, plus 4 sides * (3 verts / 1 triangle) = 12 verts / 4 triangles. Totals = 4 + 12 = 16 vertices and 2 + 4 = 6 triangles.

GLB byte size is deliberately NOT pinned here: it is asserted deterministic (byte-identical) by the runner within one kernel version, but pinning the absolute size would break on every glTF-writer upgrade without geometric meaning.
tolerance_rationale: AABB-PADDING-limited tolerance, measured first, then set (geometry-gates skill: never copy a bound blindly). Unlike the box golden (Solid.make_box, exact 1e-7 bounds), the lofted B-rep is built by OCCT's BRepOffsetAPI_ThruSections, whose faces carry the kernel modeling tolerance (~Precision::Confusion = 1e-7 mm); the OPTIMAL AABB of the resulting solid is therefore padded outward by ~1e-7 on each bound. Measured deviations vs the analytic values (2026-07-12, build123d 0.11.1 / OCCT 7.9, planegcs 0.8.0): volume 1.82e-12 mm^3 (one-ulp scale at 4e3), surface_area exactly 0.0, centroid <= 3.7e-16 mm (x/y on the axis; z exactly 7.5), and AABB padded by <= 1.0e-7 mm on all six bounds (the dominant term). Documented ceiling 2e-7 = 2x the observed worst case (1.0e-7), headroom for platform variation, and is tied to -- exactly 2x -- the standing kernel linear tolerance (1e-7 m -> 1e-7 mm at model scale). The solver contributes zero error by construction (zero-residual start, solved == input bitwise). This bound is looser than the curved cylinder goldens' 1e-9 SPECIFICALLY because ThruSections pads the AABB, not because any correctness value is imprecise (volume/area/centroid are machine-exact). Loosening it further requires a reviewed kernel-level justification recorded here and in docs/GEOMETRY-QA.md.
